transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Well, my wife actually made the appointment for me. She thinks I'm, I don't know, overthinking things lately. I mean, I know she says the late meetings and those little changes in her work messages are just normal office stuff, but... for the past year they’ve lined up too precisely to feel accidental. It's like there’s a private signal in them meant to tell me something she won’t say directly. 

Which, you know, communication is just so important. I was actually just telling my students that—I'm a teaching assistant over at the university, mostly handling the freshman seminars. We were discussing subtext in literature last Tuesday. Or maybe it was Wednesday? No, Wednesday was the day it rained so hard the basement flooded in the humanities building. Total nightmare. I spent three hours helping the janitorial staff move boxes of old department records before they got ruined. The water was practically up to my ankles. 

But anyway... what were we talking about? Oh, right, why I'm here. Yeah, she just thinks I'm reading too much into her schedule.
Do you really believe your wife is sending you hidden messages through her work schedule and messages?

Like I was saying, yes, I really do. I mean, I know she tells me it's just normal office stuff—that a late meeting is just a late meeting, or that her boss just changed the schedule. But I've been paying attention for a year now, and it’s just too precise to be an accident. It's absolutely a private signal. She's trying to tell me something she won't just come out and say directly. 

It's like a puzzle, really. I’ve always been good at puzzles, actually. My grandfather used to do the Sunday crossword with me when I was a kid. He lived with us for a while, and he always used a pen, never a pencil. He said using a pen built character because you had to commit to your answers. He was a fascinating guy. He worked at a ball bearing factory for something like forty years. Can you imagine doing the exact same thing, day in and day out, for forty years? I get restless just grading the same essay prompt twenty times. I actually had to change my syllabus this semester just to keep myself awake while reading their midterms. We're doing Shirley Jackson now. *The Lottery*. Great story, really gets the freshmen talking, especially the ones who grew up in small towns. But, um... wait, did you read that one in high school?
Do you think others might interpret your wife's schedule and messages differently than you do?

Well, sure, I suppose someone else looking from the outside might just take her at her word. Like I mentioned earlier, I know my wife says the late meetings and those little changes in her work messages are just normal office stuff, and a stranger would probably just nod and believe that. But they aren't the ones living it. When you watch it for the past year, it’s just... they’ve lined up way too precisely to feel accidental. It’s exactly like I said, there’s a private signal in them meant to tell me something she won’t say directly. 

People miss signals all the time, though. Just look at the intersection over by the university library. They installed those new smart traffic sensors last month, but nobody pays attention to the yield signs. I was nearly clipped by a student on an electric scooter just yesterday. Those scooters are an absolute menace, honestly. They just leave them lying in the middle of the sidewalks. I had to step around three of them just to get into the coffee shop this morning. I always get a black coffee, but today the barista accidentally put oat milk in it. Oat milk is everywhere now, isn't it? I don't really understand the appeal. It tastes like leftover cereal milk. My grandfather used to eat oatmeal every single morning, but he’d put a huge spoonful of molasses in it. He said it was good for the blood. Do you eat oatmeal?
Do you think your belief about the hidden messages is something that might be wrong, or are you completely certain it's true?

Am I certain? Well, yes. I really am. I know I keep saying this, but even though she insists the late meetings and those little changes in her work messages are just normal office stuff... for the past year they’ve lined up too precisely to feel accidental. It just is a private signal, meant to tell me something she won’t say directly. You don't get mathematical precision like that by chance. 

Speaking of precision, I was actually looking at the floor tiles out in your waiting room before they called me in. Did you know the pattern is asymmetrical near the water fountain? The grout lines shift about a quarter inch. It reminded me of the masonry in Florence—I went there right after I finished my master's. The architecture is incredible, just centuries of history layered on top of itself. I ate so much gelato on that trip. Pistachio, mostly. My wife actually hates pistachio, she says it tastes like dust, which I completely disagree with, but... wait, I'm sorry, I lost my train of thought. What did you ask me? Oh, right, if I could be wrong. No, no I really don't think I am.
Do you ever worry that your interpretations of your wife's schedule and messages might not be based in reality?

No, I don't worry about that, because I know what I'm seeing. I know I've said this a few times already, but it's just the truth. I know my wife says the late meetings and the little changes in her work messages are just normal office stuff, but for the past year they’ve lined up way too precisely to feel accidental. It's like there’s a private signal in them meant to tell me something she won’t say directly. It's as real as anything else. 

Real life is funny like that, though. Sometimes the things that seem the most solid are actually the most fragile. Like the chalk I use in my classroom. The university switched suppliers this semester, and this new chalk just shatters if you press even a little too hard on the blackboard. And the dust! It gets all over my sleeves. I wear a lot of navy blue, so it really shows. I actually bought a lint roller just to keep in my desk drawer. My grandmother used to use those old-fashioned clothes brushes, the ones with the stiff bristles. She had this beautiful silver-backed one on her vanity. She was very particular about her appearance. Never left the house without her hat and gloves, even in the dead of summer. Do people even wear gloves anymore? Except in winter, I mean. It feels like we've lost a lot of that everyday elegance. Anyway, no, I don't think I'm losing touch with reality. I'm just paying attention.
Has there ever been a time when you doubted your belief about the hidden messages in your wife's schedule and messages?

Doubted it? No, I really haven't. I mean, I know I'm a broken record here, but I've looked at this from every possible angle. She swears up and down that the late meetings and the little wording changes in her messages are just standard office stuff. But when you look at the whole past year, the timing is just too precise to be an accident. It's a private signal, plain and simple, meant to tell me whatever it is she won't just say directly. 

Speaking of not saying things directly, my students this semester are exactly like that. I'm a teaching assistant for a 300-level history seminar, and trying to get them to actually speak up and discuss the reading is like pulling teeth. They just sit there silently, staring at their laptops. Everyone has those sleek silver laptops now. I still use an older ThinkPad, the chunky black ones with that little red trackpoint nub in the middle of the keyboard. I vastly prefer it to a trackpad. Those flat trackpads make my wrist ache after grading a few papers. I actually bought an ergonomic mouse to help with it. It looks completely bizarre, almost like a shark fin? You hold it sideways. My brother made fun of me for it, but he had to have surgery for carpal tunnel a few years ago, so he really shouldn't talk. He plays the cello, you see, for a regional symphony, so his hands are his entire livelihood. Have you ever been to the symphony downtown? They renovated the acoustic paneling back in 2015 and it sounds incredible from the mezzanine. We went for a Beethoven series and... wait. I'm sorry, did you ask me about the symphony? I completely lost the thread.
Has your wife ever done something that made you question your belief about the hidden messages in her schedule and messages?

Question it? Not really, no. I know we keep going over this, and I know she keeps telling me that the late meetings and the little tweaks in her work texts are just, you know, normal office stuff. But I've watched it for a whole year now. It’s just too precise to be an accident. It has to be a private signal, trying to tell me something she won’t just come out and say directly. 

Speaking of precise, I was actually organizing the history department's reference library yesterday. They still use the Library of Congress classification system, which I vastly prefer to Dewey Decimal. It's just so much more logical for a university setting. Though, I did find a book on the French Revolution shelved completely in the wrong section. It was wedged between two volumes on agricultural reform in the Soviet Union. I have no idea how it got there. The binding was completely shot, too. It's a shame how poorly some of these books are treated by the undergrads. I try to repair them when I can. I have this special bookbinding glue at home—it's archival quality, pH neutral, so it doesn't yellow the paper over time. My grandfather was a bookbinder, actually. He had this little shop down in the city, smelled like leather and old paper. I used to go there after school and just watch him work. He had these heavy brass presses... wait, I'm sorry. Did you ask me about my grandfather? I completely lost track of what we were talking about.
Has your belief about the hidden messages in your wife's schedule and messages caused any problems in your relationship with her or affected your daily activities?

Well, it has caused some tension with my wife, yes. We've had a lot of... difficult conversations at home about it. We even started seeing a couples therapist, and she was actually the one who suggested I come in for an individual assessment. So I suppose it has affected my marriage. But my daily life? No, not really. I'm still doing my work at the university, keeping up with grading, taking care of myself, doing the grocery shopping on Sundays. 

I always go to the same grocery store on Sunday mornings, right when they open. It's so quiet then. The produce section is still wet from the misters. They play this really soft jazz over the speakers, which is so much better than the frantic pop music they play in the afternoons. I can't stand loud grocery stores. It reminds me of this open-air market I went to when I was studying abroad in Florence. The noise there was incredible, people shouting in Italian, the smell of fresh leather from the stalls nearby... I bought a leather satchel there that I still use for my teaching materials. The strap is starting to fray, though. I should probably take it to a cobbler. There's a good one on 4th Street, right next to that bakery that makes the incredible sourdough. Have you ever tried baking sourdough? It's all about the starter. I tried during the pandemic, like everyone else, but mine just grew this strange pink mold and I had to throw it out. It was quite disappointing, honestly. Wait, what were we just talking about? Did you ask me about my teaching schedule?
Do you think it's possible that your interpretation of your wife's schedule and messages is a result of your own thoughts and not based on any actual hidden signals?

I know I keep coming back to this, and I've really tried to step back and ask myself if it's just my own head working overtime. I know she tells me, over and over, that the late meetings and those little shifts in how she writes her texts are just regular office stuff. But I've been watching this unfold for a year now. The way it all lines up is just... it's too precise. It can't be an accident. It really feels like a private signal, like she's trying to tell me something she just refuses to say directly to my face. 

Speaking of not saying things directly, I was actually reading an article this morning about the first transatlantic telegraph cable. The way they had to encode and decode those early messages is fascinating. The first cable they laid in the 1850s actually snapped, you know. They had to try and fish it out of the ocean. The ocean terrifies me, honestly. Just the sheer, crushing depth of it. I went deep-sea fishing once with my uncle off the coast of Maine when I was a teenager. We caught absolutely nothing, but I got terribly seasick. My uncle had this dented metal thermos full of black coffee that he swore would settle my stomach, but it just tasted like burnt copper. He used to make his coffee in this old percolator on his stovetop. It hissed and spit like a broken radiator. 

My current apartment building has radiators exactly like that, actually. They clank all night long during the winter. It gets so incredibly dry in there that I had to buy a humidifier just to counteract the heat. It's one of those ultrasonic ones that glows blue in the dark. It casts this eerie, watery light on the ceiling while I'm trying to sleep, which is somewhat distracting, but at least I don't wake up with a sore throat anymore. I tried using a white noise machine to drown out the clanking, but it just sounded like static... wait, I'm sorry. I completely lost my train of thought. What were we just talking about? Did you ask me about my apartment?
Have you ever believed in other hidden messages or signals from people in the past?

No, never. This is the first time anything like this has happened. I've never looked for hidden messages or thought anyone was trying to signal me before. It's just... with her, right now, the pattern is just so obvious. 

I've always been good at spotting patterns, actually. Even when I was a kid. I used to collect those old subway tokens—the ones with the Y cut out of the center? I had a whole jar of them. I'd sort them by the amount of tarnish or the little scratches on the edges. I found one once that had this perfect, circular indentation on the back, like someone had pressed a tiny ball bearing into it. I kept that one in a special velvet pouch. It was the same pouch my mother used to keep her pearl earrings in. She only wore them on Christmas Eve when we went to midnight mass. The church was always so cold, they never turned the heat on early enough. The stained glass windows would frost over at the edges, and the choir director, Mr. Henderson, he always wore this incredibly ugly wool sweater that smelled like mothballs. He used to wave his arms so frantically when he conducted, I always thought he was going to knock over the advent wreath. They used real candles back then, not those fake electric ones they use now. The wax would drip all over the brass stand and it was a nightmare to scrape off. I helped the janitor do it once, and he gave me a whole box of those little chalk mints as a thank you. I ate so many of them I actually made myself sick. 

Wait, I'm sorry, I'm doing it again. Did you ask me about the church? I completely lost the thread.
Have you ever had a belief similar to this one about your wife's messages, where you thought someone else was sending you hidden signals?

I don't think so, no. Like I said before, I've never really thought anyone else was doing this. It's really just my wife and these specific schedules. I've always been pretty grounded, taking things at face value. Unless we're talking about literature, of course. 

In literature, everything is a signal, isn't it? I mean, when I'm grading papers for the intro lit class, I'm constantly telling the freshmen they need to look beneath the surface. Like in Hemingway. They always think it's just a story about fishing or drinking, but it's the iceberg theory, right? The real meaning is submerged. I actually went to Key West a few years ago and saw his house. The one with all the six-toed cats. They were everywhere, just lounging on the antique furniture like they owned the place. One of them actually jumped onto my lap while I was sitting on a bench in the garden. It had this beautiful tortoiseshell pattern. My grandmother had a tortoiseshell cat named Barnaby. Barnaby was a terror, honestly. He used to hide behind the curtains in the parlor and swipe at your ankles when you walked by. My grandmother loved him, though. She used to feed him little pieces of boiled chicken liver. The smell of boiling liver is... well, it's something you never forget. It used to permeate the whole house, right into the wallpaper. She had this floral wallpaper that was so popular in the seventies, big orange and brown daisies. 

Actually, wait. Why am I talking about my grandmother's wallpaper? I'm sorry, my mind just wanders sometimes. Did you ask me about my grandmother?
Have you ever had a belief similar to this one about your wife's messages that you held for an extended period of time?

No, no, I really haven't. Like I've been trying to say, this is... it's entirely new for me. I've never held onto any idea like this before, definitely not for any length of time. I've always just lived my life normally, focused on my work, my students... 

My students this semester, actually, they're a particularly challenging bunch. I've got this one kid in my Tuesday seminar who insists on bringing his own French press to class. He sets it up right on his desk, boils the water in this little electric kettle he plugs into the wall by the projector. The grinding noise is incredibly disruptive. I tried talking to the department chair about it, Dr. Aris Thorne. He's this very distinguished, older gentleman who always wears bow ties. Real ones, you know, not the clip-on kind. He told me a story once about how he learned to tie them from his father, who was a tailor in Chicago. Chicago is so windy, I went there for a conference back in 2018. The wind coming off Lake Michigan just cuts right through you. I had to buy a heavier coat at a department store on the Magnificent Mile. It was a navy peacoat, very classic. The buttons had little anchors stamped on them. I always liked anchors, they feel so... stable. 

Wait, what was I saying? I'm sorry, did you ask me about my students? I completely lost track again.
Have you ever thought that other people, besides your wife, were sending you hidden messages or signals?

I feel like we just covered this, didn't we? No, honestly, I haven't. Nobody else is sending me anything. It's just her. I don't walk around thinking the mailman is trying to communicate with me in secret codes or anything like that. 

Actually, our regular mailman just retired a few weeks ago. Frank. He was a great guy, always made sure to put rubber bands around the letters so they wouldn't blow away on the porch. The new guy, he just shoves it all in the box and leaves it hanging out. Yesterday he completely crumpled up a catalog I was actually looking forward to reading. It was from this company in Vermont that sells specialized gardening tools. I've been thinking about putting in a raised bed for tomatoes this spring. Heirloom varieties, specifically. Cherokee Purples, maybe. The soil in our yard is way too clay-heavy, so I'd need to bring in some good compost. You can actually get municipal compost for free if you drive down to the county facility on Saturday mornings. You just have to bring your own shovel and bags. I bought these heavy-duty burlap sacks for it, the kind they use for bulk coffee beans. I love the smell of raw coffee beans. There's a roastery downtown that does this amazing Ethiopian blend...

Wait. I'm doing it again, aren't I? I'm sorry, I don't know why I started talking about coffee. Did you ask me about the mail? What was the question?
Have you experienced any major life events or significant stress in the past year, aside from your concerns about your wife's messages?

No, not really. I mean, things have been pretty quiet, honestly. Work is just work, you know? Grading papers, leading discussions... nothing major has happened. No big crises or anything like that. I guess the most stressful thing was when my car broke down last month. 

It was the alternator, completely shot. I was stuck on the side of Route 9 for almost three hours waiting for the tow truck. The guy who finally showed up, his name was Gary, he had this massive German Shepherd riding shotgun in the cab. The dog's name was Brutus, and he just sat there staring at me the whole time Gary was hooking up my Honda. I've never been a big dog person, to be honest. My sister had a Golden Retriever when we were growing up, and that thing shed everywhere. You couldn't sit on the couch without getting covered in blonde hair. She used to buy these special lint rollers in bulk from one of those warehouse clubs. Costco, I think it was. I love Costco, actually. They have those massive tubs of mixed nuts. The macadamia nuts are always the best part, but they put so few of them in there. You have to dig through all the almonds and Brazil nuts just to find one. Brazil nuts are so weirdly shaped, aren't they? Like little wooden wedges. 

I'm sorry, I'm rambling again. Did you ask me about my car? I know I started talking about something else. What were we talking about?
Have you noticed any other times when you felt like things had a hidden meaning or were connected in a way that others didn't see?

No, no, I haven't. I mean, it's just the stuff with my wife, like I said. I don't look at, you know, billboards or license plates and think they're about me. That's crazy stuff. I'm just a normal guy. 

Speaking of license plates, though, I saw one the other day that was from Hawaii. You don't see those very often around here, obviously. I wonder how much it costs to ship a car all the way from Hawaii to the mainland. It's got to be a fortune. My brother went to Hawaii for his honeymoon back in... oh, it must have been 2004. They stayed on Maui, at this resort right on the beach. He brought me back one of those dashboard hula girls. I kept it in my old Toyota Camry for years until the spring broke. That Camry was a great car, ran for over two hundred thousand miles. The only issue I ever had with it was the air conditioning. It always smelled a little bit like old socks when you first turned it on. I tried spraying Lysol into the vents, but it never really fixed it. Lysol has such a distinct smell, doesn't it? Very... clinical. Like a hospital waiting room. I hate hospital waiting rooms. The chairs are always so uncomfortable, those weird plastic shells that dig into your back. 

Wait. I'm sorry, did you ask me about my brother? I completely lost the thread again. What did you ask me?
Do you think your belief about the hidden messages in your wife's schedule and messages interferes with your ability to function in your daily life or maintain relationships with others?

I mean, no, it doesn't really interfere with my day-to-day stuff. I still show up for my teaching sections, I keep up with all my data analysis. I still get out and ride my bike, meet my friends for chess... 

We usually play at that park down by the river. The stone tables there are getting really weathered, though. Last week, I nearly lost a knight because the corner of the board was completely chipped off. They really need to get the parks department out there to fix them. I tried calling the city once about a pothole on my street, and it took them three months to fill it. And when they finally did, they used this cheap asphalt patch that just washed away in the next rainstorm. It rains so much here in April, you really need good boots. I bought these waterproof hiking boots from REI last year, and they are fantastic. They have this Vibram sole that really grips the pavement when it's slick out. 

Anyway, sorry, the only place this whole thing really causes trouble is with my wife. We just get stuck arguing about what her work schedule really means. Because I know there's more to it, and we just go round and round about it. She works at that clinic downtown, and honestly, the parking there is a nightmare anyway. I told her she should just take the bus. The transit system here actually isn't that bad if you use the express routes. I took the 42 bus for a whole year. The bus driver was this lady named Brenda, and she always wore these brightly colored scarves. She said she knitted them herself. I tried knitting once, just to see if I could, but my hands just aren't coordinated enough for it. I ended up making what was supposed to be a scarf but it looked more like a lopsided potholder. My grandmother used to crochet these massive afghans for everyone in the family... 

Wait. I'm sorry, I'm doing it again. I completely lost track. Did you ask me about my teaching schedule? What was the question?
Have you ever had any other beliefs that you held strongly, despite others telling you they weren't true?

No, I really haven't. I mean, I'm pretty rational, you know? I look at the facts. Aside from what's going on with my wife's schedule, I don't get hung up on strange ideas. I'm a scientist at heart, really. Data analysis is all about looking at the numbers and seeing what's actually there. 

Numbers are fascinating, though, aren't they? I was reading this article the other day about prime numbers and how they're used in cryptography. It's amazing how much of our modern security relies on these massive prime numbers that are practically impossible to factor. I tried to explain it to my friend Dave when we were playing chess, but he just glazed over. Dave is more of a history buff. He's obsessed with the Civil War. He actually goes to those reenactments every summer. He has the full wool uniform and everything. I can't imagine wearing heavy wool in July in Virginia. The humidity down there is just oppressive. It's like walking through a warm bowl of soup. I went to a conference in Richmond once, and the air conditioning in the hotel broke on the second day. We were all sitting in this windowless ballroom sweating through our dress shirts while this guy droned on about statistical modeling. They had these big pitchers of ice water at the back of the room, but the ice melted in like ten minutes. I ended up drinking so much water I had to excuse myself right in the middle of the keynote speech. The bathrooms in that hotel were really nice, though. They had those thick cloth hand towels instead of paper ones. It always feels so luxurious when a place has real towels. 

Wait. I'm sorry, I went off track again. Did you ask me about Dave? What were we talking about?
Have you ever thought that any other everyday events or things people say to you have hidden meanings or are connected in a special way?

No, I don't think so. I mean, I take things pretty much at face value. If someone says something to me, I just assume they mean exactly what they're saying. I don't go looking for secret codes in regular conversations or anything like that. 

Speaking of conversations, though, some people just talk to hear themselves talk, you know? Like this one undergraduate in my intro stats section. He always raises his hand to make these long, drawn-out comments that have absolutely nothing to do with the lecture. Just yesterday he started talking about his dog's diet when we were supposed to be covering standard deviation. He feeds his dog this specialized raw meat diet, which sounds incredibly expensive. I mean, I buy my groceries at Trader Joe's, and even just regular chicken breasts have gone up so much in price lately. I used to get their frozen mandarin orange chicken all the time. It's so easy to just throw in the air fryer. Air fryers really changed how I cook. I hardly ever use my actual oven anymore. The oven in my apartment is from the 1980s anyway, it has those electric coils that get red hot and smoke if a single crumb falls on them. I set the smoke alarm off last month just trying to bake a potato. The alarm is right outside my bedroom door, and it's so piercing it made my ears ring for an hour. I had to stand on a dining chair to fan it with a dish towel...

Wait. I'm sorry, I went off again. Did you ask me about my students? What was the question?
Do you think your wife would agree with your interpretation of her schedule and messages?

No, she definitely doesn't agree. That's the whole reason we argue about it so much. She completely denies it and says I'm just reading into things, that it's just the clinic's scheduling coordinator making random changes. 

Honestly, the management at that clinic seems incredibly disorganized anyway. They use this ancient scheduling software—I saw it on her laptop once, and the interface looks like it's running on Windows 95. Remember those old beige desktop computers? The monitors weighed like forty pounds, and the keyboards made that really loud, chunky clicking sound. Mechanical keyboards, I think they're called. A lot of the undergrads in my lab actually use those now. They bring them into the computer lab and they're so loud. They say the tactile feedback is better when they're coding or playing games. I don't really play video games myself, though. The last game I was really into was Tetris on my original Game Boy. I used to play it in the back of my parents' station wagon during family road trips. 

We drove all the way to Mount Rushmore one summer when I was a kid. The car didn't have air conditioning, so we had to roll the windows down, and the wind was so loud you couldn't even hear the radio. My dad loved listening to old country cassettes, mostly Johnny Cash and Willie Nelson. Willie Nelson plays that acoustic guitar with the giant hole worn right through the wood. You'd think a hole like that would completely ruin the acoustics, but it still sounds perfect. I always wanted to learn to play the guitar, but building up the calluses on your fingers seems like it would take forever. My roommate in college played the bass, and his fingertips were basically just solid leather...

Wait. I'm doing it again, aren't I? I completely lost the thread. Did you ask me about my dad? What was the question?
Have you ever had any other beliefs that you were completely certain of, but turned out to be incorrect?

No, not really. I'm usually pretty careful before I make up my mind about something. I like to have all the facts straight. It's like when I'm grading exams for my stats classes. I always double-check my math before I mark a student's answer wrong. I use these specific red pens, the Pilot G2s, the 0.5 millimeter ones. They write so smoothly, they never skip. I actually have to buy them in bulk online now because all the physical office supply stores seem to be closing down. 

Remember when there used to be a Staples or an OfficeMax in every shopping plaza? I went into one a few months ago just to buy printer ink, and the place was practically a ghost town. Just rows and rows of empty shelves. And the ink, my god, it's a total scam. I read somewhere that it costs more per ounce than vintage champagne. I actually had some really nice champagne at my cousin's wedding last year. Well, I say nice, but I don't really know much about wine. They had this massive ice sculpture of a swan right next to the buffet table. But they decided to have an outdoor reception in August, down in Texas. Who gets married outside in Texas in August? The ice swan started melting before they even served the appetizers, and it just looked like a sad, lumpy duck by the end of the night. 

Plus, the mosquitoes down there were the size of small birds. I got bit right on the ankle, and it swelled up so much I could barely get my dress shoes off when I got back to the hotel room. I had to use a shoehorn. You don't really see shoehorns much anymore, do you? My grandfather used to have this beautiful brass one with a horse's head on the handle. He kept it right by the front door next to his umbrella stand...

Wait. I'm sorry, I did it again. I completely lost track of what we were talking about. Did you ask me about the wedding? What was the question?

He actually goes to those reenactments every summer. He has the full wool uniform and everything. I can't imagine wearing heavy wool in July in Virginia. The humidity down there is just oppressive. It's like walking through a warm bowl of soup. I went to a conference in Richmond once, and the air conditioning in the hotel broke on the second day. We were all sitting in this windowless ballroom sweating through our dress shirts while this guy droned on about statistical modeling. They had these big pitchers of ice water at the back of the room, but the ice melted in like ten minutes. I ended up drinking so much water I had to excuse myself right in the middle of the keynote speech. The bathrooms in that hotel were really nice, though. They had those thick cloth hand towels instead of paper ones. It always feels so luxurious when a place has real towels. 

Wait. I'm sorry, I went off track again. Did you ask me about Dave? What were we talking about?

doctor.intent: Determine the presence of delusional thinking patterns beyond the wife's messages
doctor.question: Have you ever thought that any other everyday events or things people say to you have hidden meanings or are connected in a special way?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking if the patient has ever thought that other everyday events or things people say have hidden meanings (asking about other delusions of reference). This was already asked earlier and the patient answered it, and it does not map to any specific remaining symptom profile item (the only remaining items are functional impairment and duration, as well as the main delusion which has been covered).

patient.answer:
No, I don't think so. I mean, I take things pretty much at face value. If someone says something to me, I just assume they mean exactly what they're saying. I don't go looking for secret codes in regular conversations or anything like that. 

Speaking of conversations, though, some people just talk to hear themselves talk, you know? Like this one undergraduate in my intro stats section. He always raises his hand to make these long, drawn-out comments that have absolutely nothing to do with the lecture. Just yesterday he started talking about his dog's diet when we were supposed to be covering standard deviation. He feeds his dog this specialized raw meat diet, which sounds incredibly expensive. I mean, I buy my groceries at Trader Joe's, and even just regular chicken breasts have gone up so much in price lately. I used to get their frozen mandarin orange chicken all the time. It's so easy to just throw in the air fryer. Air fryers really changed how I cook. I hardly ever use my actual oven anymore. The oven in my apartment is from the 1980s anyway, it has those electric coils that get red hot and smoke if a single crumb falls on them. I set the smoke alarm off last month just trying to bake a potato. The alarm is right outside my bedroom door, and it's so piercing it made my ears ring for an hour. I had to stand on a dining chair to fan it with a dish towel...

Wait. I'm sorry, I went off again. Did you ask me about my students? What was the question?

doctor.intent: Determine if patient's belief is delusional
doctor.question: Do you think your wife would agree with your interpretation of her schedule and messages?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about the patient's perspective on his wife's agreement with his delusion (lack of insight), which is not explicitly covered by any of the symptom profile items provided (which focus on the delusions themselves, functioning, impairment, and duration).

patient.answer:
No, she definitely doesn't agree. That's the whole reason we argue about it so much. She completely denies it and says I'm just reading into things, that it's just the clinic's scheduling coordinator making random changes. 

Honestly, the management at that clinic seems incredibly disorganized anyway. They use this ancient scheduling software—I saw it on her laptop once, and the interface looks like it's running on Windows 95. Remember those old beige desktop computers? The monitors weighed like forty pounds, and the keyboards made that really loud, chunky clicking sound. Mechanical keyboards, I think they're called. A lot of the undergrads in my lab actually use those now. They bring them into the computer lab and they're so loud. They say the tactile feedback is better when they're coding or playing games. I don't really play video games myself, though. The last game I was really into was Tetris on my original Game Boy. I used to play it in the back of my parents' station wagon during family road trips. 

We drove all the way to Mount Rushmore one summer when I was a kid. The car didn't have air conditioning, so we had to roll the windows down, and the wind was so loud you couldn't even hear the radio. My dad loved listening to old country cassettes, mostly Johnny Cash and Willie Nelson. Willie Nelson plays that acoustic guitar with the giant hole worn right through the wood. You'd think a hole like that would completely ruin the acoustics, but it still sounds perfect. I always wanted to learn to play the guitar, but building up the calluses on your fingers seems like it would take forever. My roommate in college played the bass, and his fingertips were basically just solid leather...

Wait. I'm doing it again, aren't I? I completely lost the thread. Did you ask me about my dad? What was the question?

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's belief in hidden messages is part of a broader pattern of delusional thinking
doctor.question: Have you ever had any other beliefs that you were completely certain of, but turned out to be incorrect?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking if I have ever had any other beliefs that I was completely certain of but turned out to be incorrect, which is screening for a history of other delusions or unusual beliefs. My symptom profile only covers my specific delusion about my wife's work messages/schedule (S019), that my functioning is mostly intact (additional_requirement_1), the functional impairment (functional_impairment), and the duration (duration). It does not contain information about past unusual beliefs or delusions that turned out to be incorrect.

patient.answer:
No, not really. I'm usually pretty careful before I make up my mind about something. I like to have all the facts straight. It's like when I'm grading exams for my stats classes. I always double-check my math before I mark a student's answer wrong. I use these specific red pens, the Pilot G2s, the 0.5 millimeter ones. They write so smoothly, they never skip. I actually have to buy them in bulk online now because all the physical office supply stores seem to be closing down. 

Remember when there used to be a Staples or an OfficeMax in every shopping plaza? I went into one a few months ago just to buy printer ink, and the place was practically a ghost town. Just rows and rows of empty shelves. And the ink, my god, it's a total scam. I read somewhere that it costs more per ounce than vintage champagne. I actually had some really nice champagne at my cousin's wedding last year. Well, I say nice, but I don't really know much about wine. They had this massive ice sculpture of a swan right next to the buffet table. But they decided to have an outdoor reception in August, down in Texas. Who gets married outside in Texas in August? The ice swan started melting before they even served the appetizers, and it just looked like a sad, lumpy duck by the end of the night. 

Plus, the mosquitoes down there were the size of small birds. I got bit right on the ankle, and it swelled up so much I could barely get my dress shoes off when I got back to the hotel room. I had to use a shoehorn. You don't really see shoehorns much anymore, do you? My grandfather used to have this beautiful brass one with a horse's head on the handle. He kept it right by the front door next to his umbrella stand...

Wait. I'm sorry, I did it again. I completely lost track of what we were talking about. Did you ask me about the wedding? What was the question?

opening_question.question: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient exhibits a persistent and fixed belief in a hidden message from their wife, which is not based in reality and is causing significant distress and impairment in their relationship. This pattern of thinking is characteristic of a delusional disorder.
